answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is a real Montaigne line, from his essay “Of Solitude” (De la solitude, Book I of the Essais). The French original — “La plus grande chose du monde, c’est de savoir être à soi” — is well attested. The exact English wording you see here, though, is Donald M. Frame’s 1957/58 translation; the older public-domain versions render the same sentence “to know that he is his own.”

source.excerpt: “The greatest thing in the world is to know how to belong to oneself.”
trail: The quote is genuine Montaigne: Wikiquote’s sourced section carries it with the French original and the attribution to “Of Solitude” (Book I).
HyperEssays credits this exact English phrasing — “know how to belong to oneself” — to Donald M. Frame’s translation of the French “c’est de savoir être à soi.”
The public-domain Cotton translation reads differently: “The greatest thing in the world is for a man to know that he is his own” — confirming “belong to oneself” is the modern rendering.
Frame’s The Complete Essays of Montaigne was first published by Stanford University Press in 1958 and remains in copyright.
source.excerptNote: The line sits at the core of Montaigne’s argument in “Of Solitude” that each of us should keep a private inner room — his famous arrière-boutique, or “back shop” — reserved wholly for ourselves, independent of possessions and company.
source.rightsHolder: Stanford University Press (Donald M. Frame translation, 1958)
source.rightsNote: Montaigne’s French original (Essais, first published 1580) is long in the public domain, but the exact English wording shown here is Donald M. Frame’s 1957/58 translation, published by Stanford University Press and still under copyright. The public-domain Cotton/Hazlitt translation renders the same sentence “to know that he is his own,” so this specific memorable phrasing is not itself public domain.

author.name: Michel de Montaigne
author.heading: About Michel de Montaigne
author.metaLine: 1533–1592 · French Renaissance philosopher, inventor of the essay
author.bio: Michel de Montaigne was a French Renaissance thinker and statesman who, in 1571, withdrew to his château tower to write the Essais — sprawling, self-examining pieces that effectively invented the personal essay. His subject, he said, was himself: how a person might learn to live wisely, honestly, and in possession of their own mind. “Of Solitude” is one of his most quoted essays, and this line is its distilled thesis.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: Unlike most “famous” Montaigne lines online, this one is authentic — the thought and the essay are genuinely his. The confusion is about the words.

items.why: “Know how to belong to oneself” is Frame’s 20th-century rendering of the French “être à soi.” Quote sites strip the translator’s name and present it as Montaigne’s own English, which he never wrote — he wrote in 16th-century French.

Sites that call the line “public domain” are usually thinking of the free Cotton text, which actually reads “for a man to know that he is his own” — not the “belong to oneself” wording most people quote.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is 100% Montaigne, from “Of Solitude” — but the elegant English you’re quoting is Donald Frame’s copyrighted 1958 translation, not a timeless public-domain line.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: “Of Solitude” is Montaigne’s argument that retreat is less about geography than about the mind. Wealth, status, and even loved ones can be stripped away; what remains, and what we must cultivate, is a self that can stand alone. This line is his one-sentence version of that whole essay.

Montaigne’s image for it is the arrière-boutique — a “back shop” kept wholly free, behind the storefront of our public lives, where our true liberty lives. To “belong to oneself” is to own that back room.
detailsBody: The 16th-century spelling in Montaigne’s text is “c’est de sçavoir estre à soy”; modern editions normalize it to “c’est de savoir être à soi.” The verb phrase être à soi literally means “to be one’s own / to belong to oneself,” which is why translators split between “be his own” (older) and “belong to oneself” (Frame).
context.pull: Wealth and company can be taken away; a self that can stand alone cannot.
